source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds
finding: Single-site cognitive ethnography of an MD-80 descent and landing. The cockpit system, not the pilot, remembers speeds. Bugs and speed cards turn a recall-and-read task into a judgment of spatial closeness.
numbers: Bug and flap speeds: slats only, min maneuver 177 kt; flaps 15, 152 kt; flaps 40, Vref 128 kt; no flaps or slats, 227 kt. Salmon bug base about 10 kt wide for a plus or minus 5 kt tolerance.
limits: No sample size, no error rates, no control condition. Descriptive account from observation. Author says he never saw a crew fail to set approach speeds. Shows how the system is organised, not that it is better.
agent_relevance: Guardrails should be external, lasting objects that change the task from recall to comparison.
quote: Speed bugs do not help pilots remember speeds, rather they are part of the process by which the cockpit system remembers speeds.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds (working memory and error section)
finding: Names where the pilot-held parts of the system are fragile: transposition errors when reading cards are probably the most frequent error; rehearsed speeds are open to interference; a breakdown pushes the pilot to a different strategy.
numbers: Callout required when speed varies more than 5 kt from target. Booklet uses larger type for frequent speeds and a box around Vref. Booklet set up 25-30 min before landing.
limits: The error claims are cited from Norman 1991 and Wickens and Flach 1988 and hedged as 'probably'. No error counts in this paper.
agent_relevance: Put an external check at the steps where copying slips happen (moving numbers between steps).
quote: Transposition errors are probably the most frequent sort of error committed in this process

source: Reader summary of Hutchins (1995) (ferd.ca notes)
finding: A summary that adds a design detail: engineers sized the bug base so it never covers more than one large tick mark, a benefit nobody planned. It repeats that individual pilot memory is not enhanced.
numbers: Speed zones used as bands: 0/EXT, 11-15, 28-40, Danger.
limits: Secondary summary of one paper. Weak as independent evidence; checked only against the primary text above.
agent_relevance: Fit the tolerance of a check to the tolerance of the decision it guards.
quote: Individual pilot memory has not been enhanced

source: Degani and Wiener (1991) Human factors of flight-deck checklists: the normal checklist (NASA CR-177549)
finding: First large human-factors review of the normal checklist. Says misuse or non-use of checklists is often cited in accidents. Design is shaped by regulator, maker, airline culture and the pilot.
numbers: Abstract page has no sample sizes. Gives design guidelines for normal checklists.
limits: Only the abstract page was opened. Later commentary says the related Boorman work was an accident-data review, not a controlled test of formats.
agent_relevance: Checklist form and ownership matter as much as content. Our guardrails need an owner and a stable format.

source: Haynes et al. (2009) A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality (NEJM)
finding: Before-after study of a 19-item WHO checklist in 8 hospitals in 8 cities. Deaths and complications fell.
numbers: 3,733 patients before, 3,955 after. Death 1.5% to 0.8% (P=0.003). Inpatient complications 11.0% to 7.0% (P<0.001).
limits: No control group or randomisation. Sites self-selected. Secular trend and Hawthorne effect not excluded.
agent_relevance: Upper bound on what a keenly adopted checklist can do. Expect smaller effects at scale.

source: Urbach et al. (2014) Introduction of surgical safety checklists in Ontario (NEJM)
finding: Population-wide mandatory checklist adoption gave no significant fall in deaths or complications. A failed transfer of the Haynes size of effect.
numbers: 101 hospitals; 109,341 procedures before and 106,370 after (3 months each). Mortality 0.71% to 0.65%, OR 0.91 (0.80-1.03), P=0.13. Complications 3.86% to 3.82%, OR 0.97 (0.90-1.03), P=0.29.
limits: Short 3-month windows, administrative data, natural experiment not a trial. Near-100% self-reported compliance was probably not real use (editorial view).
agent_relevance: A checklist adopted on paper but not truly used does nothing. Measure whether the agent acts on each check.

source: Bergs et al. (2014) Systematic review and meta-analysis of the WHO surgical safety checklist (Br J Surg)
finding: Pooled 7 studies of 723 screened. The checklist was linked to fewer complications and deaths, and adherence tracked with outcome.
numbers: Any complication RR 0.59 (0.47-0.74). Mortality RR 0.77 (0.60-0.98). Surgical site infection RR 0.57 (0.41-0.79). Adherence vs complications Yule's Q 0.82, P=0.042.
limits: Studies differ widely and are mostly before-after. Published before Urbach 2014, so it misses that null result. Authors ask for better studies.
agent_relevance: A dose-response with adherence supports checking that each item was done, not just listed.

source: Haugen et al. (2015) WHO checklist: stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial (Ann Surg)
finding: Best-designed trial found: randomised rollout across 5 surgical clusters in 2 Norwegian hospitals. Complications fell; the mortality drop was not significant overall.
numbers: 2,212 control vs 2,263 checklist procedures over 10 months. Complications 19.9% to 11.5%, absolute reduction 8.4 (6.3-10.5), adjusted OR 1.95 (1.59-2.40). Length of stay down 0.8 days. Mortality 1.6% to 1.0%, not significant (one hospital 1.9% to 0.2%).
limits: Two hospitals, one country, 10 months. Staff could not be blinded to the checklist.
agent_relevance: Rival evidence to Urbach: effect depends on setting and real use. Report both.

source: Reames et al. (2015) Keystone Surgery in Michigan (JAMA Surg)
finding: A statewide checklist-based surgery programme modelled on the ICU one gave no gain. A failed transfer of a famous checklist success to a new domain.
numbers: 64,891 patients, 29 hospitals, 14 with the programme. Any complication 12.4% to 13.2% (P=.26). 30-day mortality 2.1% to 1.9% (P=.32). Superficial SSI 3.2% to 3.2%. Difference-in-differences vs 15 other centres agreed.
limits: Registry data, retrospective; depth of adoption varied.
agent_relevance: A checklist that worked in one task need not transfer. Test each guardrail on our own tasks.

source: Reames et al. (2015) Keystone Surgery in Medicare patients (Med Care)
finding: Second null result for the Michigan surgery programme, with claims data on a much larger set.
numbers: 1,002,241 patients; 95 programme hospitals vs 950 matched controls. 30-day mortality RR 1.03 (0.97-1.10). Any complication RR 1.03 (0.99-1.07). Readmissions RR 1.01 (0.97-1.05). Index payments up $516.
limits: Claims data with no adherence data; Medicare patients only.
agent_relevance: Added process cost without gain. A new check should earn its cost.

source: Pronovost et al. (2006) An intervention to decrease catheter-related bloodstream infections in the ICU (NEJM)
finding: A 5-step evidence-based checklist plus culture work in 103 reporting ICUs gave a large, lasting fall in line infections.
numbers: 103 of 108 ICUs; 375,757 catheter-days. Median 2.7 to 0 per 1,000 catheter-days within 3 months. Mean 7.7 to 1.4 at 16-18 months. IRR 0.62 (0.47-0.81) at 0-3 months; 0.34 (0.23-0.50) at 16-18 months.
limits: No control group; regression to the mean and secular trend possible. Checklist was bundled with staff empowerment and feedback, so its own effect is not isolated.
agent_relevance: The checklist worked as part of a package. A scaffold needs a power to halt, not only a list.

source: Dixon-Woods et al. (2013) Matching Michigan: ethnography of the UK ICU programme (Implementation Science)
finding: An attempted copy of the Michigan ICU checklist programme in English ICUs. Local practice, not the list, decided the outcome.
numbers: 98 staff interviews; 19 ICUs observed, 17 in the programme. 1 unit transformed its practice, 5 strengthened existing efforts, 11 made little change.
limits: Qualitative. Only the abstract was opened. The programme was not an exact copy, as the authors say. Some authorship detail not verified.
agent_relevance: The same list gives different results when imposed top down. Artefact plus use practice is the unit, as Hutchins argues.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR)
finding: Asking a model to review and fix its own reasoning with no external feedback lowered accuracy. Earlier gains came from using answer labels to decide when to stop.
numbers: Accuracy (GSM8K / CommonSenseQA / HotpotQA). GPT-3.5: standard 75.9/75.8/26.0; after 1 round 75.1/38.1/25.0; after 2 rounds 74.7/41.8/25.0. GPT-4: standard 95.5/82.0/49.0; 91.5/79.5/49.0; 89.0/80.0/43.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 84.3/89.7/29.0 and GPT-4 97.5/85.5/59.0. On GSM8K, 9 responses: self-consistency 88.2 vs multi-agent debate 83.0.
limits: Fixed prompts and 2023 models. GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and changed correct to wrong more often than wrong to right.
agent_relevance: A checklist read by the model that wrote the answer is not a cockpit check. The check must bring information the writer lacked.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam and Kambhampati (2024) On the self-verification limitations of LLMs on reasoning and planning tasks
finding: GPT-4 critiquing itself collapsed; with a sound external verifier it improved a lot. Re-prompting with a verifier kept most of the gain, so the critique text was not what mattered.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Game of 24: standard 5%, LLM+LLM 3%, LLM+sound verifier 36-38%. Blocksworld: 40%, LLM+LLM 55%, sound 60-87%. Graph colouring 16%, 2%, 38%. Mystery Blocksworld 4%, 0%, 10%. LLM verifier false negative rate 20.7% (Game of 24) and 97.09% (Mystery Blocksworld).
limits: Three domains plus planning; GPT-4 of 2023-24. Verifier quality varies by domain. Chain-of-thought verification raised Game of 24 verifier accuracy from 87.0% to 98.8%.
agent_relevance: Sound external checks (code that tests) are the speed bug; self-critique is not. The gain came from the verifier signal.

source: Stechly et al. (2024) sampling baseline with a sound verifier
finding: Plain repeated sampling plus a sound checker matched or beat complex critique loops in some domains, so much of the gain is pass/fail filtering.
numbers: Game of 24: sampling k=15 28%, k=25 42% vs critique with sound verifier 36-38%. Blocksworld: k=15 68%, k=25 72% vs critique 83-87%. Self-consistency: Game of 24 6%, Blocksworld 42%.
limits: Same three-domain setup; works only where an exact checker exists.
agent_relevance: Where an exact checker exists, many tries plus the checker is a strong baseline against scaffolds.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification reduces hallucination in LLMs
finding: A fixed checklist-like loop (draft, plan check questions, answer them apart from the draft, revise) cut hallucinations. Checks answered apart from the draft worked better.
numbers: Llama 65B. Wikidata list precision 0.17 to 0.36; hallucinated entities per answer 2.95 to 0.68. MultiSpanQA F1 0.39 to 0.48. Longform FACTSCORE 55.9 baseline, 60.8 joint, 63.7 factored, 71.4 factor+revise. Llama 2 70B Chat with CoT 41.1.
limits: Base model few-shot, no retrieval. Retrieval model still better on rare facts. Chain-of-thought did not help hallucination.
agent_relevance: The check works when independent of the draft (separate context), like the second pilot reading the card.
quote: verifying questions should not attend to the original baseline response as they may be prone to repeating it

source: TICK and STICK authors (2024) TICKing all the boxes: generated checklists improve LLM evaluation and generation
finding: Model-generated YES/NO checklists per instruction raised agreement with humans. As STICK self-refinement they improved answers where vanilla Self-Refine hurt.
numbers: Pairwise agreement with humans, internal set: TICK 0.522, check-then-score 0.487, direct 0.464. Command-R+ STICK: InFoBench +6.5, WildBench +7.1, LiveBench +3.8 (Reasoning +7.8). GPT-4o LiveBench +0.8. Self-Refine -8.3 for both models. Best-of-8 WildBench 64.9 to 71.2. Krippendorff alpha 0.256 vs 0.194.
limits: Authors say checklists do not help in all settings (basic knowledge retrieval) and add cost. Gain small for the stronger model. Quality plateaued or fell by iteration four. Judge was GPT-4. Only first 100,000 characters read.
agent_relevance: Checklists beat free-form self-critique in the same setup, but the gain shrinks with a stronger model. Keep items few and instruction-specific.

source: Gao et al. (2023) PAL: program-aided language models
finding: Moving the arithmetic to a Python interpreter, with the model only writing the program, beat chain of thought. The artefact changes the task.
numbers: GSM8K: PAL Codex 72.0 vs CoT Codex 65.6. Ablation: model asked to write code and also 'run' it in text got 23.2 on GSM8K, only 4.5 above direct prompting.
limits: Math, symbolic and algorithmic tasks only; Codex-era models. Table text read from machine PDF extraction with scrambled columns; only these figures were checked.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of the speed bug: the tool does the part the model is bad at.

source: How strongly should task state influence an LLM agent? (2026 preprint)
finding: Compared showing state, a checklist, per-turn directives and a hard gate. Showing accurate state was unreliable. A gate helped when failures were state-decidable.
numbers: 3 models, 2 reasoning regimes, 2 domains. tau2-bench airline policy: 235B agent pass^1 0.39 to 0.54 with the gate; 35B agent no change. A self-written unverified ledger beat an accurate shown checklist. On PM-Bench, enforcing the matcher's judgment dropped the 35B agent below raw transcript.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed; synthetic tasks; authors not recorded.
agent_relevance: A checklist the model reads is weaker than a gate that blocks. A gate needs correct state or it hurts.
quote: Enforcement pays when failures are state-decidable and frequent, and hurts when the gate's judgement is wrong.

source: Agent skills can be harmful: skill-induced failures in LLM agents (2026 preprint)
finding: Skills that turn validation checklists into mandatory work caused failures and extra cost. Most extra procedure came from too much verification.
numbers: 307 skill-induced failures: 125 functional, 182 efficiency regressions. 67 cases from excessive verification; 30 from heavy implementation pipelines.
limits: Abstract page only. Counts are failure attributions by one tool (SkillTriage), not per-run rates.
agent_relevance: Checklists cost. Too many mandatory checks slow the agent and can cause errors. Drop items that catch no real faults.

source: CM2: checklist rewards for multi-turn, multi-step agentic tool use (2026 preprint)
finding: A checklist of binary criteria used as the reward to train a tool-using agent beat supervised fine-tuning.
numbers: 8B base model, 8k RL examples. Over the SFT version: tau-Bench +8, BFCL-V4 +10, ToolSandbox +12 points.
limits: Abstract page only. Training method, not a prompt scaffold; simulated tool environment.
agent_relevance: Checklists make good graders. They could score our own runs offline.

source: Does the way you plan matter? Planning representations for LLM web agents (2026 preprint)
finding: Four plan formats, including a checklist format, tested on hard WebArena tasks. Plan format and planner model both change success.
numbers: 4 formats: sequential subgoals, narrative, pseudocode, checklist. Agents from 3 providers. No per-format success rates seen.
limits: Only the abstract was opened; no numbers per format.
agent_relevance: The written form of a plan is a design variable; test checklist form against others on our tasks.

source: Open gap in the cockpit evidence: no discriminating experiment (this review, based on Hutchins 1995)
finding: The paper has no with-and-without comparison of bugs. Its strong claim, that memory is a property of the larger system, rests on description. Internal-representation accounts predict the same behaviour in this setting. No rival-discriminating experiment was found in this session.
numbers: None reported in the paper.
limits: Rival views (distributed representation tasks, Zhang and Norman 1994) are covered in the sibling external representations subfield and were not tested here. The search tool quota ran out before a literature check of critiques.
agent_relevance: Treat the theory as a design lens, not a proven mechanism. Prefer interventions with measured effects (sound verifier, gate).

source: Hutchins (1995) how checks are built into practice (killer items, dual cross-check)
finding: Setting approach speeds is a mandated killer item done on nearly every flight. Redundancy comes from two crew members reading the same card and bug positions, and from a callout when speed drifts. Reading and setting steps can be interleaved in many orders, and the load on memory depends on the order chosen.
numbers: Callout if speed differs by more than 5 kt from the approach speed. Booklet set up 25-30 min before landing. Author reports no crew seen failing to set approach speeds in his observations (no count given).
limits: Anecdotal, no counts. Compliance in the author's sample does not show the design is what makes it safe.
agent_relevance: Order of steps changes the memory load; fix an order for checks and make a second view (cross-check) cheap.

source: Synthesis of checklist outcome studies read this session (Haynes, Haugen, Urbach, Reames x2, Bergs)
finding: Effect sizes shrink as design gets stronger or scale grows: uncontrolled multi-country before-after shows big gains, a randomised stepped-wedge trial shows a smaller complication gain and no mortality gain, and population or statewide rollouts show none.
numbers: Complications: Haynes 11.0% to 7.0% (relative -36%); Haugen 19.9% to 11.5% (-42%, 2 hospitals); Urbach OR 0.97 (0.90-1.03), 101 hospitals; Reames Michigan 12.4% to 13.2%; Reames Medicare RR 1.03 (0.99-1.07).
limits: Different surgery populations, outcome definitions and rollout methods; no single-moderator test. Mechanism (real use vs paper use) is argued by editorialists, not measured in these studies.
agent_relevance: Expect a guardrail's measured benefit to be smaller than the first demo. Run our own controlled A/B with and without each check.
